questions.text: Walk me through how you troubleshoot a problem you have never seen before.

key_points: Reproduce first, or get enough detail to picture it: exact steps, what they expected, what happened, when it started, browser or device, and whether it affects others
Narrow systematically rather than guessing: is it this user, this account, this device, this feature, or everyone. That single question splits the problem in half
Check the known sources before inventing a theory: status page, recent releases, the knowledge base, and whether other tickets show the same pattern
Escalate with a complete package: what you tried, what you ruled out, reproduction steps, screenshots, account and ticket references. A good escalation saves the engineer an hour
strong_answer_signals: Asks whether it is one user or many, which is the fastest way to scope any issue
Escalates with evidence rather than forwarding the customer's message
Keeps the customer updated while investigating rather than going silent
avoid: Guessing at a cause and telling the customer before verifying
Escalating with no reproduction steps or context
Going quiet while you dig, which produces a second contact

questions.text: How do you document tickets, and why does it matter?

key_points: Write for the next person, not for yourself: the problem, what you verified, what you did, what you promised and by when
Tag and categorise consistently, because the tag data is what tells the company which product problems are generating contacts
Record the outcome and any commitment made, so a colleague picking it up does not contradict you
Keep it factual and professional. Customers can request records, and internal notes get read in escalations
strong_answer_signals: Connects tagging to product feedback rather than treating it as admin overhead
Documents the promise and the deadline, which is what prevents broken commitments
Writes assuming the customer may one day read it
avoid: Sparse notes such as customer called, issue resolved
Personal remarks or sarcasm in internal notes
Inconsistent tagging, which quietly destroys the reporting

questions.text: How do you handle several chats or channels at the same time?

key_points: Know your concurrency limit and be honest about it. Quality collapses past a certain number and every experienced agent knows their number
Stagger rather than parallel: while one customer is reading or testing, you progress another
Set expectations inside the chat: let me check that, I will be about two minutes. Silence in chat feels much longer than on a call
Use saved replies for the mechanical parts and write the first line yourself, so it does not read as a bot
Keep a note per conversation so you do not mix up two customers, which is the failure everyone fears
strong_answer_signals: States a real concurrency number rather than claiming unlimited capacity
Explicitly manages silence with a time estimate
Personalises the opening line even when using canned content
avoid: Claiming you can handle any number of chats at once
Copy and paste replies with no personalisation
Leaving a chat silent while working on another

questions.text: There is a major outage and the queue is flooding. What do you do?

key_points: Confirm and communicate up first: make sure the incident is known internally and that a status page or banner goes up. One public update prevents hundreds of contacts
Switch to a macro response with the facts you can share: what is affected, what is not, that it is being worked on, and when the next update comes
Give a next update time and keep it, even if the update is that there is no news. Silence is what turns frustration into anger
Triage inside the flood: customers with a deadline, safety or payment impact still need individual handling
After recovery: proactive follow-up to the affected customers, and feed the contact volume into the incident review
strong_answer_signals: Prioritises the mass communication before the individual replies
Commits to an update time rather than a fix time
Follows up after recovery instead of just closing the tickets
avoid: Guessing at a restore time you cannot control
Answering hundreds of tickets individually while nothing goes out publicly

questions.text: Someone contacts you asking for access to an account. How do you verify them?

key_points: Follow the verification process exactly, every time, including for someone who sounds legitimate, angry or senior. Social engineering relies on exceptions
Verify with what the process requires, and never accept information that is easy to find publicly as proof on its own
Watch the pressure signals: urgency, a story about why the normal method will not work, requests to change the recovery email, phone or bank details
For any change to payment or recovery details, use an independent call-back or the account's existing verified channel, never the contact details supplied in the request
If it fails verification, say what they can do instead and escalate suspicious attempts to security
strong_answer_signals: Refuses to bypass verification for a sympathetic or forceful caller
Names urgency and detail changes as the classic social engineering pattern
Reports the attempt rather than simply declining it
avoid: Making an exception because the person is upset or claims seniority
Accepting publicly available information as identity proof
Not escalating a suspected takeover attempt

questions.text: How do you handle personal and payment data in a support conversation?

key_points: Collect the minimum you need, and never ask for a full card number, CVV or password. No legitimate process requires an agent to see them
If a customer volunteers card details in chat or email, stop them, do not record it, and move to the secure method
Know the frame you work under: PCI DSS for card data, HIPAA for health data in the US, PIPEDA and provincial law in Canada, GDPR for EU residents
Access only the records you need for the case you are handling. Looking up an account out of curiosity is a terminable offence in most companies
Handle deletion and access requests through the defined process rather than ad hoc
strong_answer_signals: Stops a customer from sharing card details rather than accepting them politely
Knows that curiosity lookups are logged and disciplinary
Names the relevant regime for their jurisdiction
avoid: Ever asking for a password to help someone
Copying sensitive data into a ticket note
Sharing account information with a family member without authorisation

questions.text: Tell me about a time you did not know the answer.

key_points: Say plainly that you told the customer you did not know rather than improvising. Improvising is how support loses trust permanently
What you actually said: I want to give you the right answer rather than a fast one, let me check and come back to you by [time]
How you found it: knowledge base, a colleague, the specialist team, the documentation, testing it yourself
You came back when you said you would, even if the answer was only progress
What you did afterwards so the next person does not hit the same gap: wrote it up, added it to the knowledge base
strong_answer_signals: Comfortable saying I do not know without treating it as failure
Gave a specific callback time and met it
Closed the knowledge gap for the team rather than only for themselves
avoid: Passing the customer to someone else with no context
Promising to come back and not doing it

questions.text: Tell me about a time you received critical feedback on a call or ticket.

key_points: Pick real feedback from a quality review, a manager, or a customer survey comment, and state what it actually said
Your first reaction honestly, then how you got past it and looked at the evidence, usually the recording or the transcript
The specific change you made, not a general intention to do better: a different opening, an explicit summary before closing, slowing down, checking understanding
Evidence it worked: your scores, a later review, a customer comment
Say that you now ask for feedback rather than waiting for it
strong_answer_signals: Listens to their own recordings, which very few people do voluntarily
Names one concrete behavioural change rather than an attitude change
Treats quality review as coaching rather than surveillance
avoid: Defensiveness, or explaining why the reviewer was wrong
Feedback so mild it clearly was not criticism

questions.text: Tell me about a time you helped a teammate or a new agent.

key_points: Name the gap: product knowledge, confidence on the phone, handling an angry customer, or falling behind on volume
How you helped without taking over: listened to a call together, walked through the tool, gave them your notes, took a ticket to free them up
The moment you handed it back so they could do it themselves next time
The outcome for them and for the team, and if you can, the retention angle: new agents who feel supported stay
Say if you became a buddy, mentor or trainer as a result
strong_answer_signals: Builds the skill rather than solving it for them
Understands new hire attrition is the expensive kind for a support manager
Approaches it privately and without condescension
avoid: Covering for a genuine competency or conduct problem

questions.text: A customer becomes abusive toward you personally. What do you do?

key_points: Separate frustration from abuse. Shouting about the problem is frustration and you work through it. Slurs, threats and personal attacks are abuse and different rules apply
Stay calm and do not match their tone. Give one clear warning in the wording your company uses: I want to help you, and I need us to keep this respectful or I will have to end the contact
If it continues, end the contact as your policy allows, and document exactly what was said in their words
Tell your supervisor. Abuse is under reported because agents absorb it, and a pattern only becomes visible if it is logged
Take a moment before the next contact rather than carrying it into the queue
strong_answer_signals: Draws a clear line between anger and abuse
Knows the policy for ending a contact and uses it
Reports it rather than treating abuse as part of the job
avoid: Absorbing abuse silently to protect a metric
Responding in kind or hanging up without a warning
Carrying the emotion straight into the next customer

questions.text: A customer threatens to sue you or to post about this publicly. How do you respond?

key_points: Do not argue, do not admit liability, and do not promise an outcome. Keep helping with the underlying problem, which is usually still solvable
Escalate immediately per policy. Legal threats go to a supervisor and often to legal; public threats usually involve the social or PR team
Keep the tone unchanged and professional. A threat does not earn worse service, and it does not earn special treatment either
Document precisely what was said, with quotes and timestamps
For public posts, follow the company's response process rather than replying personally, and keep the resolution attempt in a private channel
strong_answer_signals: Keeps working the actual problem rather than reacting to the threat
Escalates without letting the threat change what is offered
Documents verbatim, which is what legal will need
avoid: Saying anything that reads as accepting fault
Offering compensation to make the threat go away

questions.text: A customer has difficulty communicating with you, through language or a disability. How do you handle it?

key_points: Slow down, simplify the words but not the respect. Never raise your voice or speak to them as though they are a child
Use the tools available: interpretation services, chat or email instead of voice, TTY or relay services, and accessible formats where required
Confirm understanding by asking them to tell you the next step in their own words rather than asking whether they understood
Give extra time and stay patient. Handle time is the wrong metric for this contact and a good manager knows it
Know that accessibility is a legal obligation in North America, under the ADA in the US and the AODA and provincial standards in Canada
strong_answer_signals: Uses professional interpretation rather than improvising or relying on a family member
Checks understanding by asking them to restate, not by asking do you understand
Treats accessibility as an obligation, not a favour
avoid: Speaking louder or more slowly in a patronising way
Rushing to protect a handle time target

questions.text: You realise you gave a customer wrong information. What do you do?

key_points: Contact them proactively and fast. Hoping they will not notice is the worst option and the one that turns a mistake into a complaint
Say it plainly and own it: I gave you incorrect information yesterday, here is what is actually true, and here is what I am doing about it
Fix the consequence, not just the fact: if they acted on your bad information, deal with that too, and escalate if you need authority you do not have
Tell your supervisor before the customer does
Find the cause: outdated knowledge base, unclear policy, or your own gap, and correct it so it does not repeat
strong_answer_signals: Proactive contact rather than waiting to be caught
Fixes the downstream consequence, not only the statement
Tells the manager first, which is what protects the team
avoid: Quietly correcting it and hoping nobody noticed
Blaming the knowledge base or a colleague to the customer
Waiting for them to raise it

questions.text: How do you staff and schedule a support team to the volume?

key_points: Forecast from history by day and by half hour, then layer on what you know is coming: a release, a campaign, a billing run, a seasonal peak
Convert volume to required agents using handle time and target service level, then add shrinkage for breaks, training, meetings, absence and attrition. Shrinkage is where most schedules fail
Watch occupancy, not just headcount. Sustained high occupancy burns people out and turnover then makes the staffing worse
Flex with part time, staggered starts, a float pool, and cross-trained agents rather than mandating overtime as the default
Track adherence fairly, and measure forecast accuracy so the plan improves rather than repeating the same error
strong_answer_signals: Names shrinkage and occupancy without prompting, which marks real contact centre experience
Treats sustained overtime as a symptom rather than a solution
avoid: Scheduling a flat team across a spiky demand curve
Pushing occupancy high to look efficient
No plan for the known peaks

questions.text: One of your agents is consistently below target. How do you handle it?

key_points: Look at the data before the conversation, and look at the right data. Low volume with high quality is a different problem from high volume with low quality
Separate the cause: a skill gap, a tools or process problem, workload and schedule, or something outside work. Ask before telling
Build a specific plan with dates: side by side coaching, call reviews together, a knowledge refresh, a mentor, and a measurable expectation
Follow up when you said you would. An improvement plan with no follow-up is just a warning
If it does not change, move to the formal process with documentation from the first conversation, and involve HR early
strong_answer_signals: Checks whether the system is the problem before blaming the person
Coaches with recordings rather than with metrics alone
Documents from the first conversation, not from the first warning
avoid: Managing by dashboard without ever listening to their calls
Public criticism or comparison to other agents
Letting it run for months without a conversation

questions.text: Support has high turnover. How would you reduce it?

key_points: Measure honestly: overall and first ninety day turnover, and cut it by team and by manager. New hire attrition and one bad manager are the two usual stories
Fix the daily reality first: realistic occupancy, breaks that actually happen, working tools, current knowledge base, and authority to resolve without escalating everything
Protect people from abuse. Agents leave over unaddressed abusive customers more often than employers realise
Give a path: specialist, escalations, QA, training, or a route into product, sales or technical teams. A dead end job is a job people leave
Onboard properly with a gradual ramp and a buddy, since most attrition happens in the first weeks
Close the loop visibly on something the team raised
strong_answer_signals: Separates first ninety day attrition from overall
Names abuse handling and agent authority as retention levers
Understands the cost: rehiring and retraining usually exceeds the cost of fixing the cause
avoid: Blaming the labour market or the generation
Ignoring that turnover in support is often a management problem

questions.text: Why do you want to work here specifically?

key_points: Name something real about them: their product, their customers, an experience you had with their support, their reputation for how they treat the team
If you have used the product, say so and say what you noticed. That is the strongest opening a support candidate has
Connect it to what you want: product depth, a technical support path, a customer base you find interesting
Say what you bring that shortens their ramp: tool experience, the channel, the industry, a language
strong_answer_signals: Has used the product and can describe the experience
Something that could only be said about this employer
Two directional rather than only what they want
avoid: Pay and schedule as the leading reason
Not knowing what the company actually sells

questions.text: Where do you see yourself in a few years?

key_points: Commit to doing this role well first, and say what you want to master in it: the product, the hardest contact types, the tooling
Then a direction that exists inside their organisation: senior or escalation agent, QA, training, team lead, or a move into technical support, customer success or product
Be honest if you want to move out of frontline support eventually. Managers know most people do, and hiding it damages trust later
Tie the growth to what the team gains from it
strong_answer_signals: Names a real internal path rather than a vague ambition
Honest about wanting to progress beyond the frontline
Shows they intend to stay long enough to be worth training
avoid: Making it obvious the role is a stopgap
No ambition at all, which reads as disengaged
A plan with nothing to do with this employer

questions.text: How do you handle the emotional demands of support work?

key_points: Acknowledge it honestly. Absorbing other people's frustration all day is real emotional labour, and pretending otherwise is not credible
Separate the complaint from yourself. They are angry at the situation, and taking it personally is what burns people out
Name what you actually do: a reset between hard contacts, taking your breaks properly, talking to a colleague, physical activity, and a real boundary at the end of a shift
Use the formal supports where they exist, including employee assistance programmes
Say when you would raise it with a manager rather than quietly running down
strong_answer_signals: Realistic rather than heroic about the demands
Has a concrete reset habit between contacts
Willing to say when they need support
avoid: No strategy at all, which reads as a burnout risk
Describing customers with contempt as the coping mechanism

questions.text: Why are you leaving your current role?

key_points: Answer forward: the product or industry you want, growth, a channel, a schedule that fits your life, a team you can learn from
If the real reason is genuinely bad, such as unmanageable volume or an unsupportive manager, state it factually once without a list of grievances
Never name individuals and never relitigate a conflict
Move straight into why this role fits
strong_answer_signals: Neutral and brief about the previous employer
A reason this employer can actually satisfy
Consistent with the dates on the resume
avoid: Criticising managers, customers or the company
Being so vague it invites suspicion

questions.text: What questions do you have for us?

key_points: Ask about the daily reality: what is the contact volume per agent, what is the target, and how often is it hit
Ask about readiness: how long is training before live contacts, and what support exists when you are stuck
Ask about quality and authority: how is quality scored and by whom, and what can an agent resolve without escalating
Ask about the team: turnover, the path out of this role, and how the company handles abusive customers
Close by asking what makes someone successful in the first six months and what the next steps are
strong_answer_signals: Asks how abusive customers are handled, which shows real experience and self respect
Asks about agent authority, since low authority is the main driver of both bad service and turnover
avoid: Only asking about pay, breaks and time off in a first interview
Questions already answered in the posting
